why_wrong: A. Labelling after the round risks mixing up tubes between patients. B. Labelling away from the patient breaks the link with positive identification. D. Pre-labelled tubes can easily be used for the wrong patient. E. The laboratory cannot verify which patient a sample came from.
pearl: Most laboratories will reject a transfusion sample that is unlabelled, incompletely labelled or does not match the request form, and the sample must be retaken.
thinking: Several patients to bleed ↓ Risk of tube mix-up ↓ Identify patient at bedside ↓ Label immediately after sampling ↓ One patient at a time
exam_trap: D, Pre-labelling all the tubes — it seems efficient, but tubes labelled away from the patient are easily used for the wrong person.
takeaway: Label samples at the bedside immediately after collection, after positively identifying the patient.

stem:
A 50-year-old woman receives her first invitation for breast screening and phones her GP surgery, unsure whether to go. She asks the nurse if the test is guaranteed to find any cancer.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Tell her that screening has no downsides, so she should attend
options.B: Explain that an abnormal result means she definitely has cancer
options.C: Explain that attending is expected of every registered woman
options.D: Discuss the benefits, the possibility of false results and overdiagnosis, and support her own choice
options.E: Describe the benefits only, to avoid putting her off

correct_answer: D. Discuss the benefits, the possibility of false results and overdiagnosis, and support her own choice
why_correct: Screening is offered, not required, and people should be helped to make an informed choice. That means explaining the potential benefit of early detection alongside the limitations, including false-positive results, missed cancers and overdiagnosis of conditions that might never have caused harm. Her decision should then be respected.
why_wrong: A. All screening carries potential harms. B. An abnormal screening result needs further tests and does not confirm a diagnosis. C. Participation is voluntary and has no bearing on registration. E. Withholding information about harms prevents informed choice.
pearl: Overdiagnosis, detecting a condition that would never have caused symptoms in a person's lifetime, is a key harm of screening and leads to unnecessary treatment.
thinking: Screening invitation ↓ Patient uncertain ↓ No test is perfect ↓ Explain benefits and harms ↓ Support an informed, voluntary choice
exam_trap: E, Describing the benefits only — it may seem kind and may raise uptake, but omitting the harms undermines informed consent.
takeaway: Screening participation should be an informed choice based on both benefits and harms.

stem:
A 47-year-old man is seen in the surgical outpatient clinic with a small, easily reducible right inguinal hernia that causes him only occasional mild discomfort. The surgeon considers that either watchful waiting or a planned mesh repair would be reasonable, each with different advantages and drawbacks.

How should the decision be made?

options.A: Book whichever option the surgeon thinks best and tell him afterwards
options.B: Ask his wife which option she would prefer for him
options.C: Hand him two leaflets and let him decide without discussion
options.D: Explore his priorities, explain the benefits, risks and uncertainties of each, and agree a plan together
options.E: Recommend the surgeon's favoured option and mention the alternative only briefly

correct_answer: D. Explore his priorities, explain the benefits, risks and uncertainties of each, and agree a plan together
why_correct: When more than one reasonable option exists, shared decision-making is expected: the clinician brings knowledge of benefits, harms and uncertainties (for example the small risk of incarceration with watchful waiting versus surgical complications and chronic groin pain after repair), the patient brings his values and preferences, and they reach a decision together. This is set out in NICE guidance on shared decision-making and GMC guidance on decision making and consent.
why_wrong: A. Deciding for him without discussion ignores his autonomy. B. A relative cannot decide for an adult with capacity. C. Written information supports, but does not replace, a two-way discussion. E. Steering him towards one option without balanced information is not shared decision-making.
pearl: Decision aids and asking what matters most to the patient are practical tools that improve the quality of shared decisions.
thinking: Two reasonable options ↓ Each with trade-offs ↓ Patient values matter ↓ Explain benefits, harms and uncertainty ↓ Decide together
exam_trap: E, Recommending the surgeon's favoured option — it seems helpful to give a clear lead, but presenting the alternative only briefly denies him a balanced choice.
takeaway: Where reasonable options exist, explain the trade-offs and make the decision together with the patient.
notes: Reviewer fix: Replaced knee OA exercise-vs-steroid-injection pair (NICE NG226 makes exercise core and injection adjunct, so not genuine equipoise) with minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia: watchful waiting vs mesh repair; options/explanations updated

stem:
Before a planned colonoscopy, a 58-year-old retired teacher has a discussion with the endoscopist about why it is advised, the chance of bleeding or perforation, and the option of a CT colonography instead. She asks questions, has time to think, and then freely chooses to go ahead.

Which ethical and legal concept does this illustrate?

options.A: Paternalism
options.B: Implied consent
options.C: Best-interests decision
options.D: Undue influence
options.E: Informed consent

correct_answer: E. Informed consent
why_correct: For consent to be valid, the person must have capacity, be given sufficient information about the procedure, its material risks and reasonable alternatives, and decide voluntarily. All three elements are present here, so this is informed consent, consistent with the Montgomery ruling and GMC guidance.
why_wrong: A. Paternalism is the clinician deciding for the patient. B. Implied consent is inferred from behaviour, such as offering an arm, and is not appropriate for an invasive procedure with significant risks. C. Best-interests decisions are only made for people who lack capacity. D. Nothing suggests pressure that overrides her free choice.
pearl: Since Montgomery (2015), doctors must disclose any material risk, judged by what a reasonable person in the patient's position, or this particular patient, would want to know.
thinking: Capacity present ↓ Information on risks and alternatives given ↓ Time to ask questions ↓ Decision made freely ↓ Informed consent
exam_trap: B, Implied consent — she is cooperating with a planned procedure, but implied consent applies only to minor acts; here the explicit discussion of risks and alternatives makes this informed consent.
takeaway: Valid consent requires capacity, adequate information and a voluntary decision.

stem:
A practice nurse finishes giving an influenza vaccine in a busy flu clinic. The sharps container is on the trolley within reach.

What is the safest way to deal with the used needle and syringe?

options.A: Place them directly into the sharps container straight away, without recapping
options.B: Recap the needle carefully with both hands before discarding
options.C: Put them in a tray and clear it at the end of the clinic
options.D: Pass them to a healthcare assistant to dispose of
options.E: Drop them into the clinical waste bag

correct_answer: A. Place them directly into the sharps container straight away, without recapping
why_correct: Used sharps should be discarded immediately, at the point of use, into a sharps container by the person who used them, and needles should not be recapped. This minimises handling and is required under the Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013 to reduce needlestick injuries.
why_wrong: B. Two-handed recapping is a common cause of needlestick injury. C. Leaving sharps in a tray increases handling and risk to others. D. Passing sharps to another person exposes them to injury; the user is responsible for disposal. E. Waste bags are not puncture-resistant.
pearl: After a needlestick injury, encourage the wound to bleed, wash with soap and running water, do not scrub or suck it, then report promptly so post-exposure prophylaxis can be considered.
thinking: Sharp used ↓ Minimise handling ↓ Do not recap ↓ Sharps bin at point of use ↓ User disposes immediately
exam_trap: B, Recapping carefully with both hands — it feels like it makes the needle safer, but recapping is one of the commonest ways needlestick injuries happen.
takeaway: Dispose of used needles immediately at the point of use into a sharps container without recapping.

stem:
A school nurse refers a 9-year-old girl to the GP. She has head lice and impetigo that have not been treated for months, often comes to school without breakfast in a thin summer coat during winter, and has missed several dental and hospital appointments. Letters to her parents have gone unanswered.

What should the GP recognise?

options.A: This is within the normal range of parenting
options.B: The girl most likely has a primary eating disorder
options.C: The parents should be warned they will be prosecuted
options.D: No action is needed unless the child asks for help
options.E: A possible safeguarding concern about neglect that needs assessment and referral

correct_answer: E. A possible safeguarding concern about neglect that needs assessment and referral
why_correct: Persistent failure to meet a child's basic needs for food, clothing, hygiene and healthcare, together with missed appointments and disengaged parents, are recognised features of neglect. NICE guidance on child maltreatment advises considering or suspecting neglect in this situation and following local safeguarding procedures, which may include referral to children's social care.
why_wrong: A. A sustained pattern of unmet basic needs is not normal variation. B. Hunger and untreated infections point to neglect rather than a psychiatric disorder. C. A safeguarding response focuses on the child's welfare, not punishment. D. Children rarely ask for help, and waiting would leave her at risk.
pearl: Neglect is the commonest reason for a child being subject to a child protection plan in England.
thinking: Several unmet basic needs ↓ Untreated health problems and missed appointments ↓ Parents not engaging ↓ Pattern suggests neglect ↓ Follow safeguarding procedures
exam_trap: A, Normal range of parenting — individual findings may seem minor, but the persistent combination of unmet needs is the hallmark of neglect.
takeaway: A persistent pattern of unmet basic and healthcare needs should prompt safeguarding action for neglect.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman with a small, early-stage breast cancer is told by the surgeon that mastectomy and breast-conserving surgery followed by radiotherapy give similar long-term survival. She lives on a remote island with a long journey to the nearest radiotherapy unit and is the main carer for her mother.

When the options are being discussed with her, which consideration should carry most weight in reaching the choice?

options.A: The operation the breast unit performs most frequently
options.B: The procedure the consultant surgeon personally favours
options.C: Her own priorities, values and practical circumstances
options.D: The option that costs the hospital trust least
options.E: The view of her adult son, who has accompanied her

correct_answer: C. Her own priorities, values and practical circumstances
why_correct: When two treatments offer similar outcomes, the right choice depends on what matters to the individual patient. Her travel burden, caring role and her own feelings about the options are exactly the factors that shared decision-making brings into the discussion. GMC guidance on decision making and consent and NICE NG197 expect the clinician to explain the options and support her to choose in line with her values.
why_wrong: A. How often a unit performs an operation does not reflect what suits this particular patient. B. The surgeon's personal preference should inform but not replace her own choice between reasonable options. D. Cost to the trust is not a basis for choosing between equally effective treatments for an individual patient. E. A competent adult makes her own decision; a relative's view can be heard only if she wishes.
pearl: NICE NG197 recommends decision aids and the 'teach-back' approach to check that patients have understood the risks and benefits of each option.
thinking: Two reasonable treatments with equivalent survival ↓ No single clinically superior choice ↓ Her geography and caring duties change the practical burden ↓ Values and circumstances decide between equal options ↓ Support her to choose
exam_trap: B, The consultant's preferred procedure — expert opinion feels authoritative, but when options are clinically equivalent the clinician's role is to inform, not to choose for the patient.
takeaway: When treatments are equally effective, the patient's own values and circumstances should determine the choice.

stem:
At a urology clinic, a 66-year-old retired engineer with low-risk localised prostate cancer is weighing up active surveillance against radical treatment. He says he is confused because the two approaches seem to carry quite different side effects and uncertainties.

Which principle should guide the consultation?

options.A: Advise the option the urologist would pick if he were the patient
options.B: Explain each option with its benefits, risks and uncertainties and help him decide
options.C: Recommend radical treatment as the most modern and definitive approach
options.D: Ask his wife to make the choice so that he is spared the worry
options.E: Select active surveillance for him because it carries the fewest side effects

correct_answer: B. Explain each option with its benefits, risks and uncertainties and help him decide
why_correct: This is a preference-sensitive decision: both options are reasonable and each trades different benefits against different harms such as incontinence or erectile dysfunction versus the need for repeated monitoring. Shared decision-making means setting out the options, their risks and uncertainties in terms he understands and supporting him to reach a choice that fits his values (GMC decision making and consent; NICE NG197).
why_wrong: A. The doctor's own hypothetical choice reflects the doctor's values, not the patient's. C. Newer or more definitive treatment is not automatically better, and it carries significant side effects. D. A capacitous adult decides for himself; his wife can support him but cannot decide on his behalf. E. Choosing the lowest-harm option for him excludes him from a decision that depends on what he values.
pearl: Low-risk localised prostate cancer is a classic preference-sensitive decision, as survival is similar across active surveillance and radical treatment.
thinking: Two reasonable management options ↓ Different side-effect profiles and uncertainties ↓ No objectively correct choice ↓ Explain benefits, risks and uncertainties clearly ↓ Support him to choose according to his values
exam_trap: E, Choosing active surveillance for him — it sounds protective because it avoids treatment side effects, but making the decision on his behalf removes his involvement and may not match his priorities.
takeaway: For preference-sensitive decisions, explain the options and their trade-offs and let the patient choose.

presentation: Possible physical abuse of an older adult
stem:
During a home visit, a GP reviews an 86-year-old man with moderate dementia who lives with his daughter-in-law. There are oval bruises of different colours on the inner aspects of both upper arms. He takes no anticoagulant or antiplatelet medicines, and a recent full blood count was normal. Nobody can explain how the bruises happened, and he becomes tearful and withdrawn whenever she comes into the room.

What is the most likely explanation that needs to be considered?

options.A: Senile purpura from fragile skin
options.B: Possible physical abuse requiring safeguarding assessment
options.C: Bruising from unwitnessed falls related to dementia
options.D: Bruising caused by an undiagnosed bleeding disorder
options.E: Scurvy from poor dietary intake

correct_answer: B. Possible physical abuse requiring safeguarding assessment
why_correct: Bilateral bruises on the inner upper arms look like grip marks, and they are of different ages with no explanation. Combined with fear and withdrawal in the presence of a carer, this pattern raises concern about physical abuse. Under the Care Act 2014 the GP should consider abuse, document carefully and raise an adult safeguarding concern rather than attribute the findings to ageing.
why_wrong: A. Senile purpura usually affects the backs of the hands and forearms and does not explain fear of a carer. C. Falls typically injure bony prominences such as the face, hips and outer limbs rather than the inner upper arms. D. A normal blood count and no antithrombotic drugs make a bleeding cause unlikely, and it would not explain his behaviour. E. Scurvy causes perifollicular haemorrhages and gum changes rather than grip-shaped bruises.
pearl: Bruising on protected sites such as the inner arms, inner thighs, ears and neck should always raise concern about non-accidental injury at any age.
thinking: Bruises of different ages with no explanation ↓ Grip-mark pattern on inner upper arms ↓ No anticoagulants and normal blood count ↓ Fear of a particular carer ↓ Consider abuse and raise a safeguarding concern
exam_trap: C, Bruising from unwitnessed falls — falls are common in dementia and offer a comfortable explanation, but they do not produce symmetrical inner-arm bruising or explain fear of one person.
takeaway: Unexplained bruising on protected sites plus fear of a carer should prompt consideration of abuse.

presentation: Multiple bruises in a young child
stem:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to his GP with a cough. While listening to his chest, the GP notices bruises over his back, behind both ears and on his cheeks, some yellow-green and others fresh and purple. His mother says he is a clumsy child who bumps into things. He is otherwise well and developing normally.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Note the bruises and arrange a routine review in a month
options.B: Ask the health visitor to check on the family at home
options.C: Arrange a clotting screen and decide on referral when results are back
options.D: Follow local child safeguarding procedures and refer the same day
options.E: Tell the mother that the bruises suggest someone is hurting him

correct_answer: D. Follow local child safeguarding procedures and refer the same day
why_correct: Bruises of different ages on the ears, cheeks and back are in sites rarely injured by ordinary childhood falls, and 'clumsiness' does not account for them. NICE CG89 says this pattern should make the clinician suspect maltreatment, so the GP must follow local safeguarding procedures and refer to children's social care without delay. Medical tests such as a clotting screen can be organised as part of the assessment but must not hold up the referral.
why_wrong: A. Waiting a month could leave the child exposed to further harm. B. Informal monitoring by a health visitor is not a substitute for a formal safeguarding referral. C. Investigations may be part of the work-up but deferring referral until results return delays protection. E. Confronting the parent may increase risk to the child and could compromise any investigation.
pearl: Ears, cheeks, neck, back and buttocks are uncommon sites for accidental bruising in children; shins, knees and the forehead are typical accidental sites.
thinking: Multiple bruises of different ages ↓ Unusual sites: ears, cheeks, back ↓ Explanation of clumsiness does not fit ↓ Suspect maltreatment (NICE CG89) ↓ Refer through safeguarding procedures now
exam_trap: C, Doing a clotting screen first — excluding a bleeding disorder seems thorough, but it must run alongside, not before, the safeguarding referral.
takeaway: Unexplained bruises of different ages in unusual sites need a same-day safeguarding referral, with tests arranged in parallel.

stem:
An 8-year-old girl attends the emergency department for the third time in two months, this time with a burn on her forearm. Previous visits were for a wrist injury and a scalp laceration, each with a different account from her stepfather, who has brought her in on every occasion. She is quiet and says nothing about how the injuries happened. A nurse suggests waiting until the girl tells someone what is going on.

What should the doctor do?

options.A: Treat the burn, discharge her and keep a brief record
options.B: Wait until she makes a disclosure before taking further action
options.C: Promise her that anything she says will be kept secret
options.D: Ask the stepfather directly whether he has been hurting her
options.E: Recognise the pattern as a safeguarding concern and follow safeguarding procedures

correct_answer: E. Recognise the pattern as a safeguarding concern and follow safeguarding procedures
why_correct: Repeated attendances with different injuries and changing explanations are recognised alerting features for maltreatment. Children often do not disclose abuse, so the doctor must act on the pattern itself by documenting carefully, checking previous attendances and following local safeguarding procedures (NICE CG89; GMC protecting children and young people).
why_wrong: A. Treating and discharging without escalation ignores the pattern and may leave her at risk. B. Waiting for a disclosure delays protection; many children never disclose. C. Confidentiality cannot be promised when a child may be at risk of harm. D. Confronting the carer may increase the risk to the child and is not the doctor's role.
pearl: A child does not need to say anything for a safeguarding concern to be raised; frequent attendances and inconsistent histories are enough.
thinking: Third attendance in a short period ↓ Different injuries and changing accounts ↓ Child silent, no disclosure ↓ Disclosure is not required to act ↓ Follow safeguarding procedures
exam_trap: B, Waiting for her to disclose — it seems respectful and avoids accusation, but abused children frequently stay silent and delay leaves her exposed.
takeaway: Act on a concerning pattern of injuries; do not wait for a child to disclose abuse.

stem:
Parents bring their 4-month-old daughter to an urgent care centre because they noticed a bruise on her thigh after a nap. They think she must have rolled against the bars of her cot. She cannot yet roll over or crawl, and she is feeding well and appears comfortable.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Accept the explanation and reassure the parents
options.B: Document the bruise and check it again at her next routine review
options.C: Arrange a clotting screen and discharge if it is normal
options.D: Treat this as a safeguarding concern and arrange urgent paediatric assessment
options.E: Advise the parents to pad the cot and return if more bruises appear

correct_answer: D. Treat this as a safeguarding concern and arrange urgent paediatric assessment
why_correct: Bruising in a baby who is not yet independently mobile is uncommon and must be regarded as a possible sign of physical abuse. The proposed mechanism is not possible for an infant who cannot roll. Local safeguarding procedures for bruising in non-mobile babies require urgent paediatric assessment, including investigations, alongside a safeguarding referral (NICE CG89).
why_wrong: A. The explanation does not fit her developmental stage, so accepting it would miss possible abuse. B. Deferring review could leave the infant at risk of serious further injury. C. A normal clotting screen does not explain the bruise or remove the safeguarding concern. E. Practical advice treats the bruise as accidental when the account is developmentally implausible.
pearl: Those who do not cruise rarely bruise: any bruise in a non-mobile infant needs safeguarding assessment.
thinking: Bruise on a 4-month-old ↓ Infant cannot roll or crawl ↓ Mechanism given is developmentally impossible ↓ Non-mobile infant bruising protocol ↓ Urgent paediatric and safeguarding assessment
exam_trap: C, A clotting screen then discharge — investigations are part of the work-up, but a normal result does not make an unexplained bruise in a non-mobile baby safe.
takeaway: Any bruise in a non-mobile infant is a safeguarding concern until proven otherwise.

stem:
On the second day after a hip replacement, a 71-year-old woman has a painful, distended bladder and a bladder scan confirms urinary retention. The foundation doctor is preparing to insert a urethral catheter on the ward.

Which approach is essential for this procedure?

options.A: Explain the procedure, obtain her consent and use aseptic technique
options.B: Use a clean non-sterile technique so the procedure is quicker
options.C: Choose a wide-bore catheter to reduce the chance of blockage
options.D: Insert the catheter first and explain it once she is comfortable
options.E: Leave the catheter in place until discharge to avoid repeat retention

correct_answer: A. Explain the procedure, obtain her consent and use aseptic technique
why_correct: Catheterisation is an invasive procedure, so she needs an explanation and valid consent beforehand. Aseptic technique reduces the risk of catheter-associated urinary tract infection, one of the commonest healthcare-associated infections. NICE guidance on infection prevention also advises using the smallest suitable catheter and reviewing the need for it regularly.
why_wrong: B. A non-sterile technique increases the risk of catheter-associated infection. C. The smallest catheter that drains effectively should be used to limit urethral trauma. D. Explaining afterwards means consent was not obtained. E. Catheters should be removed as soon as they are no longer needed, because infection risk rises with duration.
pearl: The risk of catheter-associated bacteriuria rises with every day a catheter stays in, so its continued need should be reviewed daily.
thinking: Clear indication: urinary retention ↓ Invasive procedure needs explanation and consent ↓ Aseptic technique prevents infection ↓ Smallest suitable catheter ↓ Remove as soon as no longer needed
exam_trap: B, A clean non-sterile technique — it is faster on a busy ward, but it raises the risk of catheter-associated urinary infection.
takeaway: Urethral catheterisation needs consent, aseptic technique, the smallest suitable catheter and prompt removal.
